definition: A lightweight, isolated box that packages an app together with everything it needs to run (its dependencies, config, and files), so it runs the same way anywhere without needing its own full operating system.

The core part of an operating system that talks directly to the hardware and manages processes, memory, and files. A container shares the host machine's kernel instead of running its own, which is what keeps it lightweight and fast to start.

Short for virtual machine — a simulated computer, complete with its own full operating system, running on top of your real one. It's much heavier and slower to start than a container, which shares the host's kernel instead of carrying a whole OS.

The background program that actually does the work of creating, running, and stopping your containers. You never talk to it directly — the docker command sends it instructions, and it carries them out.
Short for command-line interface — the docker command you type in a terminal. It's how you control Docker: it sends your instructions to the Docker daemon, which does the actual work.
A read-only template that bundles an app with everything it needs to run. Running (starting) an image creates a container from it, and doing so never changes the original image itself.

The command that creates and starts a new container from an image. If the image isn't already on your machine, docker run downloads (pulls) it automatically first, so you never have to pull it yourself beforehand.
The command that downloads an image from a registry, like Docker Hub, onto your machine without starting a container from it.
The command that shuts down a running container without deleting it — the container and its data stay on disk until you remove it with a separate command.
The command that permanently deletes a stopped container from your machine. Adding the -f flag force-removes it even if it's still running.
Docker's default public registry — an online library of ready-made images, like nginx or redis, that anyone can download with docker pull or start directly with docker run.
A server that stores container images so you can upload (push) or download (pull) them instead of rebuilding everything from scratch every time. Docker Hub is the most common public example.
One step of an image, stacked on top of the previous ones. Docker caches each layer and skips rebuilding the ones that haven't changed, which is what makes repeat builds so much faster.
A plain-text file that lists, step by step, the exact instructions Docker follows to build an image — what to start from, what files to add, and what to run.
The Dockerfile instruction that sets the base image everything else in the file builds on top of. Every Dockerfile needs one, usually as its very first line.
The Dockerfile instruction that copies files from your own project folder into the image being built, e.g. copying your app's source code so it's baked in and available once the container starts.
The Dockerfile instruction that executes a command, like installing a package, while the image is being built, and bakes the result permanently into the image.
The Dockerfile instruction that sets the command a container runs automatically the moment it starts. Unlike RUN, which only fires while the image is being built, CMD only fires at container startup.
The command that reads a Dockerfile's instructions and turns them into an actual image. Its -t flag lets you name (tag) the resulting image, like -t myapp, so you can find and run it later.

A Dockerfile technique that uses one stage to compile or build your app with all its heavy build tools, then copies only the finished result into a lean final stage — so the image you actually ship stays small.
A label attached to an image, like myapp:1.2, that identifies a specific version — so you can pin exactly which build you want to run instead of grabbing whatever happens to be newest.

An ordinary tag name that many images use by default. It doesn't automatically mean the newest version — it only moves to whatever was most recently pushed under that name — so relying on it in production doesn't guarantee you're running the newest code.

A way of linking one specific folder on your host machine directly into a container, so the container reads and writes real files that live on the host and survive even after the container is removed.
Storage that Docker creates and manages for you, rather than you pointing it at a folder yourself like a bind mount. Its data survives even after the container using it is deleted.

A virtual network Docker sets up so containers can talk to each other. Every container gets its own network by default, but containers placed on the same shared network can reach each other simply by name.
The command that runs something, like opening a shell, inside a container that's already running. It attaches to that existing container instead of starting a new one.
The command that shows a container's console output — everything it has printed since it started — useful for checking what it's actually been doing.
The command that returns a container's full configuration, formatted as JSON, including details like its network settings and mounted volumes.
A setting, controlled by the --restart flag (e.g. --restart unless-stopped), that tells Docker whether to automatically start a container back up after it crashes or the host reboots.
A tool for defining and starting several related containers together, like an app and its database, with a single command instead of running separate docker run commands for each one.
The YAML file where you describe a Compose setup. Under its top-level services key, you list each container you want, along with its image, ports, and environment variables.
A plain-text format for writing structured configuration data using indentation instead of brackets — it's the format docker-compose.yml is written in.
The top-level section of a docker-compose.yml file where you list each container you want Compose to manage, each with its own image, ports, and settings.

The starting image a Dockerfile builds on top of, set by its FROM line. Picking a small, well-maintained one keeps your final image lean and avoids dragging in someone else's unpatched vulnerabilities.
All the possible points where a system could be broken into or exploited. A smaller, slimmer base image contains fewer unnecessary programs and files, which shrinks this.

The full set of files in your project folder that gets sent to the Docker daemon before a build starts, so instructions like COPY have something to pull from. A large build context (e.g. a folder full of unneeded logs or dependencies) slows the build down, which is exactly what a .dockerignore file trims.

A regular, limited-permission user account rather than the all-powerful root/admin account. Containers run as root by default, so explicitly switching to a non-root user limits the damage possible if the container is ever compromised.
A registry that restricts who can see or download its images, unlike Docker Hub, which is public by default. It's typically used so only a company's own team can access its images.
The command that uploads a local image to a registry so others (or other machines) can pull it down.

A cleanup command that removes unused Docker resources — stopped containers, unused networks, and dangling images (leftover images with no tag pointing to them, usually from a rebuild) — that pile up over time and quietly eat disk space.
A tool that manages containers across many machines for you — automatically scheduling where they run, restarting the ones that crash, and scaling them up or down as needed.
The most widely used container orchestrator — a system that automatically schedules, restarts, and scales containers across a whole cluster of machines.
